newsitem.title: CAMBODIA: Cambodia passes weak environmental law.
newsitem.headline: Cambodia passes weak environmental law.

text.p: Parliament passed Cambodia's first environmental law on Monday, but analysts said the legislation was too weak to tackle the country's environmental problems.
"This law won't make any difference. It is so weak, I have trouble thinking it even has symbolic significance," said an analyst working in Cambodia's environmental sector.
Minister of Environment Mok Mareth told Reuters he believed the spirit of the law, which contains general provisions for natural resource management, was significant nonetheless.
"This law is very important because it focuses on protecting the quality of the environment in Cambodia," he said.

The law contains requirements for a national environmental plan, environmental impact assessments of development, evaluation of natural resources and the creation of an environmental fund from government and international aid.
It says violators of the law will be sent a warning letter and can be fined up to $20,000 or be imprisoned for up to three years.
But analysts said the law was gutted as it moved through the political process.

"It gives the Ministry of Environment no authority to do anything new," the analyst said. "Even though the law does provide for some basic sanctions, most will only result in a written order and nothing more."

Cambodia's environmental practices have been under fire by watchdog groups, who have accused the government of ignoring the impact of growing development, logging and mining in its haste to bring revenue to the war-torn country.

Fishing resources, mangroves and air quality have declined, and logging companies have been granted concessions to harvest many of Cambodia's forests, which have dwindled rapidly, according to the Environment Ministry.
Last week, the International Monetary Fund cancelled a $20 million loan to Cambodia, citing concern over the country's forestry policies and accounting for logging revenues.
Most of the international community's attention has focused on the forestry code, however, leaving the environment law largely forgotten, analysts said.
As a result, the government was under no pressure to create tough legislation on natural resources management and enforcement of environmental standards, they noted.
